name: Dextrose / maltodextrin

lead: Dextrose is single-unit glucose, and maltodextrin is a short chain of glucose units. Both digest quickly, so lifters mix them into drinks during or after training to supply fuel and replenish glycogen.
The appearance chain is more training energy and recovery, leading to more muscle over time.

paras: Mixed with water as an intra-workout or post-workout drink, often alongside protein or creatine.
Maltodextrin has a glycemic index around 110, so large amounts spike blood sugar; people with diabetes or insulin resistance are cautioned.

web.title: ISSN position stand: diets and body composition

chain: More training volume and recovery, more muscle
angle.text: Lifters use carbohydrate powders around workouts to fuel sessions and aid recovery, which supports muscle growth.

lead: Dextrose is another name for D-glucose, and maltodextrin is a family of glucose chains of roughly three to 17 units made from starch. [1][2] Both digest quickly, so lifters mix them into drinks before, during or after training to supply fuel and refill muscle glycogen. [2]

The appearance chain is indirect: more available training energy and faster glycogen refilling can support more training volume and recovery, which over time supports muscle growth. Maltodextrin has a glycemic index listed at 110, above glucose at 100. [2]

Research on carbohydrate timing is mixed in emphasis: a 2013 review by Aragon and Schoenfeld argues the urgency of post-workout carbohydrate is often overstated for people not training the same muscles twice a day, and that total daily carbohydrate matters most. [3]

paras: Dextrose is the monosaccharide glucose; the monohydrate form (about 9.5% water) is common in foods and drink mixes, and anhydrous dextrose is used in medical applications such as glucose tolerance tests. [1] Glucose was first isolated from raisins by Andreas Marggraf in 1747, and Friedrich August Kekule proposed the name dextrose because its solutions rotate polarized light to the right. [1]

Digestible maltodextrin is made by boiling plant starch (corn in the US, wheat in Europe) and treating it with acid and enzymes. It supplies about 4 calories per gram and is rated by dextrose equivalent (DE) on a 3 to 20 scale, where higher DE means shorter chains, more sweetness and more solubility. A digestion-resistant type, developed in the 1990s, behaves as a soluble fibre instead. [2] Digestible maltodextrin was first produced between 1967 and 1973. [2]

Athletes use digestible maltodextrin for rapid energy, to replenish glycogen and during prolonged exercise; it also appears in oral rinses studied for performance. [2] Lifters commonly pair these powders with protein or creatine in a shake.

Aragon and Schoenfeld note that immediate carbohydrate intake produces glycogen supercompensation and that delaying it two hours can cut resynthesis rate by as much as half, but that glycogen is essentially fully replenished within 24 hours even with delayed intake. They state rapid repletion matters mainly for endurance athletes with under about 8 hours between depleting sessions, or those training the same muscles twice in a day. [3] In their review, adding carbohydrate to ample protein gave no further benefit to muscle protein synthesis in the studies cited. [3]

The 2017 ISSN review of diets and body composition reports that carbohydrate restriction can impair performance, and that in untrained subjects doing resistance training a high-carbohydrate surplus produced mostly lean mass with little fat gain. [4]

Maltodextrin is considered generally recognised as safe (GRAS) as a food ingredient in the US. Large amounts of digestible maltodextrin can spike blood sugar, which Wikipedia flags as a particular concern for people with diabetes or insulin resistance, and excess intake may contribute to weight gain, reduced insulin sensitivity and higher blood lipids. [2] Digestion-resistant versions can cause bloating and gas. [2] Wheat-derived maltodextrin is exempt from wheat allergen labelling in the EU but not the US. [2]

A randomized trial in older adults with type 2 diabetes compared resistance training with carbohydrate or protein supplementation, reporting on blood glucose, lipids and hypertrophy. [5] A trial in trained young adults examined creatine and caffeine during resistance training. [6] Reviews of nutrient timing and of diets for body composition are summarised above. [3][4]

lore.intro: On T Nation forum threads, lifters discuss maltodextrin and dextrose as post-workout or intra-workout carbohydrates and as ingredients in mass gainers, with mixed personal tolerance. [7][8]

claims.claim: Dextrose and maltodextrin are key to replenishing muscle glycogen and creating an insulin spike after training.
Large servings of maltodextrin can sit badly in the gut.

timeline.event: Andreas Marggraf isolates glucose from raisins. [1]
Johann Tobias Lowitz finds glucose in grapes. [1]
Aragon and Schoenfeld publish a review of nutrient timing, including post-exercise carbohydrate. [3]
The ISSN publishes its review on diets and body composition. [4]
